title: SYNTHONY: A Stress-Aware, Intent-Conditioned Agent for Deep Tabular Generative Models Selection
summary: Treats the choice of tabular synthesizer as the problem worth automating rather than the supply of synthesizers, profiling a dataset along four interpretable stress dimensions - long-tailed marginals, high-cardinality categoricals, Zipfian imbalance and small-sample size - and matching that profile against a capability registry to pick a generator that minimizes regret against an intent-specific oracle, given a user preference over fidelity, privacy and utility. SDV is both prior art and pool: it is named twice as the open-source library that democratized access to individual synthesizers and provides unified APIs and benchmarking but leaves model selection to the user, which is the gap the selection layer fills, it is credited for Gaussian Copulas in the statistical lineage, and TVAE is one of the ten candidate synthesizers the framework selects among.
evidence: the introduction states that current open-source libraries such as SDV (Patki et al. 2016) and SynthCity have made significant strides in democratizing access to individual synthesizers but function as collections of independent building blocks rather than intelligent selection systems, leaving users to navigate the trade-offs manually; section 2.2 states that SDV and SynthCity provide unified APIs and benchmarking but require manual hyperparameter specification and still leave model selection to the user, and that this work introduces an automated selection layer above them; section 2.1 traces the lineage from statistical methods including Gaussian Copulas (Patki et al. 2016) through CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) to diffusion models; the experimental setup lists a pool of ten candidate synthesizers across four categories with TVAE among the deep generative group, alongside AIM, DPCART, AutoDiff, TabDDPM, NFlow, ARF, CART, BayesianNetwork and SMOTE. Importance 3: TVAE is one of ten generators in the selection pool and SDV is described rather than run.

title: Generative Synthetic Data for Causal Inference: Pitfalls, Remedies, and Opportunities
summary: Shows that a tabular synthesizer can pass distributional, privacy and train-on-synthetic-test-on-real checks while still distorting the average treatment effect, because prediction loss penalizes treatment-effect error only through an overlap-weighted term, so a generator can reproduce dominant observed outcomes while underlearning the intervention-relevant contrast; it formalizes the mismatch with sensitivity and loss-decomposition results and proposes a hybrid alternative that generates covariates with a generative model but fits the treatment and outcome mechanisms separately, then uses the result as a pre-analysis simulation engine for comparing OR, IPW, AIPW and TMLE estimators. CTGAN is one of the two generators the whole empirical program runs on, supplying both the fully generative arm and the covariate generator inside the proposed hybrid, and is credited in the related work for introducing conditional GANs with mode-specific normalization and training-by-sampling.
evidence: the related-work section states that for tabular data CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) introduced conditional GANs with mode-specific normalization and training-by-sampling; section 3 names GAN-based approaches citing Xu et al. 2019 as one of the two families whose causal fidelity is in question; the ACTG application constructs four synthetic datasets named LLM Full, LLM Hybrid, CTGAN Full and CTGAN Hybrid, and the results table reports each on train-on-synthetic-test-on-real RMSE for the cd420 outcome, mean distance to the closest record, and IPW, AIPW and TMLE treatment-effect estimates; the abstract states that LLM-based hybrid synthesis is often more faithful than CTGAN where causal fidelity can be assessed. Importance 4 on the GAN_BERT precedent: CTGAN runs unmodified as the covariate generator inside the paper's own proposed hybrid framework, not only as a comparison arm, so half the empirical results are CTGAN output and the work does not stand without it.

title: Generating Logically Consistent Synthetic Supply Chain Data with LLM-Driven Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Argues that synthetic supply chain records must preserve the operational logic governing them - temporal orderings, arithmetic dependencies, hierarchical taxonomies and conditional rules - and not only their marginal distributions, and builds a framework that first extracts a column relationship knowledge graph using a multi-LLM ensemble with majority voting and then conditions generation on that graph, so that generated records satisfy the discovered constraints rather than merely resembling real ones statistically. CTGAN is one of four compared generators, included as the widely adopted GAN-based framework for tabular synthesis alongside TabDDPM, TabSyn and GReaT.
evidence: section 2.1 names existing deep generative models for tabular data including GAN-based approaches such as CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) and argues they are optimized to preserve marginals, correlations and downstream predictive utility rather than operational logic; section 2.2 places CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) and CTAB-GAN+ as the GAN-based direction in the evolution of deep tabular methods; section 4.2 states that the framework is compared against four representative state-of-the-art tabular generative baselines and that CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) is included as a widely adopted GAN-based framework for tabular data synthesis, with TabDDPM, TabSyn and GReaT the other three. Importance 3: a compared generator among four, with none of CTGAN's machinery adopted. Same Cambridge group as paper-inter-column-logic-eval-2025 and a direct continuation of it - that paper proposed the inter-column logic metrics, this one builds a generator to satisfy them - so the two are best reviewed together.
